name: Serial Reasoning
blurb: A sequence runs across the rows and down the columns.
childIntro: Look for a sequence of shapes that repeats. It runs across every row and down every column. What is missing?
howItWorks: Pearson describes this as recognising a sequence of shapes, such as circle then square then triangle, and how the sequence changes across the rows and down the columns. It is usually a three by three grid. It is harder than an analogy because the child has to hold a repeating cycle in mind rather than a single change.
parentTip: The hard version has two things cycling at once on different lengths, for example a shape cycle of three and a colour cycle of two. Then the pattern does not repeat cleanly row by row. If your child is stuck, get them to read the whole grid as one long line, left to right and top to bottom, instead of row by row.

questions.prompt: What goes in the empty box?

figure.alt: A grid where every row goes circle, square, triangle. The last box is empty.

questions.explanation: Every row goes circle, square, triangle. The bottom row has a circle and a square already, so a triangle comes next.
questions.strategy: Read one full row out loud. Then read the row with the hole and stop where the hole is.

questions.prompt: What belongs in the empty box?

figure.alt: A three by three grid of shapes with the bottom right box empty.

questions.explanation: Two things decide the answer. Each column keeps the same shape, and each row has its own color. The empty box is in the last column and the bottom row, so it is a blue arrow. Choice b takes its look from the wrong row.
questions.strategy: Point along the row and say what changes. Then point down the column and do the same.
